formal.statement: ∀ (m n : ℤ), Int.fib (m + n) = Int.fib (m - 1) * Int.fib n + Int.fib m * Int.fib (n + 1)

notes:
Closed in-tree. The sizing that blocked this was correct in one direction and too pessimistic in the other.

CORRECT: it does NOT reduce to Nat.fib_add plus sign bookkeeping. Nat.fib_add (fib (succ (m+n)) = fib m * fib n + fib (succ m) * fib (succ n)) is exactly this statement restricted to m >= 1 and n >= 0 -- one of four constructor pairs, and not even all of the non-negative case, because at m = 0 the leading coefficient is fib(-1), a value at a NEGATIVE index. The proof uses Nat.fib_add nowhere.

TOO PESSIMISTIC: the blocking combinator was cheap. Int.induction_on (two-sided induction over the integers, int_prelude/two_sided_induction.rs) is two Nat.rec inductions in which every bridging step is PURE REDUCTION -- add (ofNat k) one reduces to ofNat (succ k) because Nat.add recurses on its right argument and that argument is the literal 1; sub (negSucc k) one reduces to negSucc (succ k) the same way; sub zero one reduces to negSucc 0 through subNatNat's closed Nat.sub 1 0. No equation lemma, no Nat.sub truncation, no natAbs detour. The combinator, Int.fib_rec and this theorem were each accepted by the kernel on the first attempt.

Fibonacci is a two-step recurrence, so no single-index motive can step; the motive is Q k := P k and P (k+1), the pairing device nat_prelude/fibonacci.rs already uses for Nat.fib_add. The step ingredient is Int.fib_rec, the recurrence at EVERY integer index. The downward step is stated as an addition and closed by an add_right_cancel helper rather than by subtracting, so no difference is ever formed, and the second component of Q (n-1) is P n transported along (n-1)+1 = n, which is not definitionally the same index for symbolic n.
